heading_ja: 親文字群中の文字（添え字付き）（cl-21）

cases.quote: In this document, superscripts and subscripts and their base characters are handled as ornamented character complex (cl-21) characters.
cases.rationale: § A.21 has no table. Its whole body is one sentence — EN 'Any character may participate in ornamented character complex.', JA 「どの文字も添え字付きの親文字群中の文字として使うことができる．」 — so no code point is a member and no code point is excluded, and the quoted sentence of § 3.7.1 is the only place in the document that says what makes an occurrence one: it sits in a complex of a base character (親文字) with its superscripts or subscripts (添え字). This case declares that complex over all three occurrences and asks about the base character, because the quoted sentence names the base character explicitly and an implementation that reads cl-21 as 'the small ones' answers the ornament correctly and this item wrongly. § 3.9.2's own entry for cl-21 carries no descriptive paragraph at all, only the JIS X 4051 naming Note, which is why § 3.7.1 is cited beside it.

forbidden.why: Classifying the occurrence by its code point and ignoring the construct it was declared in. U+0048 is listed in § A.27 as proportionally-spaced, which is the frame declared here, so a table-only lookup answers cl-27 for this item — and would answer cl-27 for every character of every ornamented character complex, leaving cl-21 unreachable. § A.21 lists nothing precisely so that the construct decides.

cases.quote: In this document, superscripts and subscripts and their base characters are handled as ornamented character complex (cl-21) characters.
cases.rationale: The same input, asking about the subscript. Both ends of the complex are cl-21 and the quoted sentence names them in one breath, so this case and the one before it are one assertion seen from its two ends. The ornament is declared on the second size, six tenths of the base: § 3.7.1 leaves the character size (文字サイズ) and the block-direction position 'implementation definable parameters' per JIS X 4051 and only recommends 'around 60%', so the ratio is the caller's declaration and nothing here asserts it. Nothing about the smaller size is what makes this occurrence cl-21, which the twin case A.21/superscript-two/no-construct-declared states from the other side.

forbidden.why: Reading the digit as a grouped numeral (連数字). § A.24 lists U+0032 with the Remark 'half-width' (字幅は半角) and this occurrence declares the proportional frame, and no grouped numeral is declared over it; the occurrence is in an ornamented character complex, which § 3.7.1 says is what decides.

cases.quote: Between a subscript or superscript and an adjacent base character (preceding or following) (see Figure 87), or between base characters with ornament characters, or between ornament characters themselves. The reason is that these character sequences are to be handled as one object.
cases.rationale: The third occurrence of the same complex carries no ornament of its own. § 3.7.1 says 'superscripts and subscripts and their base characters', plural, and § 3.1.10's ninth item — quoted here — names a boundary 'between base characters with ornament characters', which only exists if a run of base characters is one complex rather than one base per ornament. So a base character inside the run is cl-21 whether or not an ornament hangs on it, and an implementation that classifies only the immediate neighbors of an ornament answers this item wrongly and then finds a break opportunity in the middle of H2O.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in ornamented character complex. — JA: どの文字も添え字付きの親文字群中の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: The differential twin of A.21/ornamented-complex/base-character, and the reason that case is worth publishing: the two inputs are byte-identical apart from the `constructs` object, including the smaller declared size on the middle occurrence, and they must answer differently. § A.21 enumerates nothing, so no scan over the appendix tables can ever produce cl-21 and nothing about a code point, an advance or a declared size makes an occurrence a member. With no complex declared, U+0048 is classified from the tables: § A.19 lists it as the folded key of the full-width Ｈ and § A.25 and § A.27 list it as proportionally-spaced, the proportional frame declared here rules out the full-width reading, and cl-25 is itself a construct membership no unit symbol has been declared for — so cl-27 is what is left standing.

forbidden.why: Inferring the complex from the sizes. The middle occurrence is declared at six tenths of the base size here exactly as it is in the complex case, and that is not what § 3.7.1 conditions the class on; a caller may set any character smaller for any reason. An implementation that answers cl-21 here has made the class a property of the caller's metrics, which ADR 0002 makes the caller's own.

cases.quote: Superscripts and subscripts are usually set after the base character, with some exceptions for chemical formulae (which appear before the base character). They should be set solid.
cases.rationale: The mass number of an isotope is set before its element symbol, and the quoted sentence is the document's own exception. The complex here is ornament-then-base rather than base-then-ornament, and the first occurrence — the one a reader meets before any base character — is cl-21 all the same. An implementation that recognizes an ornament by looking backwards for a base character finds none and falls through to the code-point tables, answering cl-27 for this item. The Japanese half states the exception twice, once for 上付き文字 and once for 下付き文字, so both directions of ornament carry it.

cases.quote: When both the superscript and the subscript follow the base character, usually the subscript is set first and set solid, followed by the superscript set with solid spacing. For chemical formulae sometimes both superscript and subscript are set vertically in the same position with respect to the base character, and with solid spacing between them and the base character.
cases.rationale: One base character carrying two ornaments, in the order the quoted Note calls usual: the subscript first, then the superscript. The class of the second ornament is the assertion — a complex is not a pair, and an implementation that models it as base-plus-one-ornament answers this item outside any complex. The Note also states where the two ornaments sit and that both spacings are solid (ベタ組); that is placement rather than class and this case asserts none of it, which is why the input declares only the range and lets the caller's own advances stand.

cases.quote: Western characters (cl-27) — ² 00B2 SUPERSCRIPT TWO 上付き2 — Remarks: proportionally-spaced / プロポーショナル
cases.rationale: The boundary the document draws around this class, in the one place a reader is most likely to cross it. U+00B2 is typographically a superscript, the Japanese common-name column of § A.27 calls it 上付き2 in so many words, and it is a member of cl-27 and of no other Appendix A table — the appendix names it once. Being a superscript glyph is therefore not being an ornamented character complex character: § A.21 lists nothing, and § 3.7.1 conditions cl-21 on the complex an occurrence sits in, not on the shape of the glyph. An implementation that seeded cl-21 from the Unicode superscript block, or from a font's 'sups' feature, answers cl-21 here and diverges from § A.27 on a character the appendix does list.

forbidden.why: Deriving cl-21 from the code point. § A.21's whole body is 'Any character may participate in ornamented character complex.', which grants a permission and lists no member; § A.27 lists U+00B2. A class whose section enumerates nothing cannot be reached by a table lookup at all, and an implementation that reaches it there has invented a membership the document does not state.

cases.quote: Any character may participate in ornamented character complex.
cases.rationale: The same two occurrences, with the complex declared, and the answer changes. Read with the case above, this pair is the whole of what § A.21 says: the same code point is cl-27 in running text and cl-21 in a complex, and nothing in the stream but the declaration distinguishes them. 'Any character' is not a courtesy — it is why the section has no table, and it means an implementation cannot pre-compute cl-21 membership for any code point, in either direction.

cases.quote: Grouped numerals (cl-24) — 2 0032 DIGIT TWO — Remarks: half-width / 字幅は半角
cases.rationale: § A.21 publishes no table and therefore no Remarks column, so the character frame (字幅) draws no distinction inside this class — which is exactly what has to be shown, because for this code point it draws every distinction outside it. Appendix A names U+0032 four times and the frame is what separates the readings: half-width under § A.24, the folded full-width ２ under § A.19, proportional under § A.27. This case declares the half-em frame, the frame that would make the occurrence a grouped numeral, and the answer is cl-21. Its full-em twin declares the frame that would make it cl-19 and answers the same thing, and the two cases differ in nothing else — which is the assertion, and the reason they are checked as one.

forbidden.why: Letting the frame decide a class the construct has already decided. The half-em frame is § A.24's Remark for U+0032 and is why this frame was chosen for this case; § 3.7.1 makes every character of an ornamented character complex cl-21, and § A.21 states no Remark that could qualify it.

cases.rationale: The frame twin. § A.19 prints the full-width ２ and the Appendix A preamble's folding keys it on U+0032, so a caller declaring the full em has declared the occurrence § A.19 lists; the same declaration outside a complex answers cl-19 rather than cl-24. Inside one it answers cl-21, identically to the half-em case, and every expected value below is byte-identical to that case's. An implementation that consults the frame before the construct answers cl-24 there and cl-19 here and fails both, which a single frame would not have shown.

forbidden.why: The same error as the half-em case makes with the other answer. § A.19 lists the full-width digit and the full-em frame names it, so an implementation that reaches the tables at all reaches cl-19 here; § 3.7.1 says the occurrence is cl-21 because of where it sits.

cases.quote: In this document, superscripts and subscripts and their base characters are handled as ornamented character complex (cl-21) characters.
cases.rationale: The complex declared here covers the last three occurrences and not the first. The quoted sentence says which occurrences are cl-21 — the ornaments and their base characters — and says nothing about their neighbors, so a hiragana standing before a complex is cl-15 exactly as it would be anywhere else. This is the boundary of the construct read as a boundary of the class: an implementation that colors a whole stream, or a whole word, from one declaration answers cl-21 here and then sets ordinary Japanese text solid against everything, because § B.2 note 9 hands every cl-21 pair to § 3.7.1.

forbidden.why: Extending the complex past the range the caller declared. § 3.7.1 names the ornaments and their base characters and nothing else, and § A.15 lists U+3042; an occurrence adjacent to a complex is not in it.

cases.quote: The name of this class in JIS X 4051 is "Characters included in ornamented base characters complex". The meaning of "base characters complex" is characters in a complex including ruby, ornament characters and emphasis dots.
cases.rationale: The quoted Note is § 3.9.2's own gloss on cl-21 and it is the trap: a base characters complex (親文字群) is defined there as covering ruby, ornament characters and emphasis dots, so a reader who takes the Note as the membership condition makes every emphasized or ruby-annotated character cl-21. The name it glosses says otherwise — JIS X 4051 calls the class 添え字付き親文字群中の文字, the complex *with ornaments* — and JLReq gives the other two their own classes, cl-22 and cl-23, and gives emphasis none at all: § 3.3.9 refers to the emphasized text by the classes it already has, 'symbols placed alongside a run of ideographic character (cl-19) or hiragana (cl-15) characters'. So an emphasis-dot (圏点) construct declared over a hiragana leaves it cl-15. This is what the class is not, stated where the document itself invites the confusion.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (3.9.2 and its cl-21 Note, 3.3.9, A.15)

forbidden.why: Reading § 3.9.2's Note as the membership condition. The Note explains what 親文字群 means in the JIS name; the JIS name is 添え字付き親文字群中の文字, and § 3.7.1 conditions the class on superscripts and subscripts. Emphasis dots are neither, and the document assigns them no class of their own.

cases.quote: In vertical writing mode, characters with superscripts or subscripts, that is ornamented character complex (cl-21) characters, are rotated 90 degrees clock-wise. If the length of the sequence is short enough, the sequence can be set as tate-chu-yoko.
cases.rationale: The only sentence in the document that mentions cl-21 and a writing direction in one breath, and it changes no class: rotation is where the glyphs are drawn, and the quoted Note calls the rotated characters cl-21 characters while it rotates them. So membership in this class is direction-invariant, and this case is the same declaration as A.21/ornamented-complex/base-character with the direction stated. The Note's second clause is a permitted alternative to the rotation, not a second class: a sequence set as tate-chu-yoko (縦中横) is a tate-chu-yoko, which § A.30 gives its own class, and which a caller declares as that construct instead of this one. No policy question in the generated space selects between them, because the choice is a declaration the caller makes rather than a knob an implementation turns; that is recorded here rather than written as a second permitted answer nothing could select.

forbidden.why: Reading the Note's tate-chu-yoko clause as a reclassification. The clause says the sequence 'can be set as' tate-chu-yoko, which is a caller's decision to declare a different construct — § A.30's — and not something a vertical direction does to a complex the caller declared as ornamented. An implementation that switches class on the direction alone answers cl-30 for every short cl-21 run in vertical text.

cases.quote: It is prohibited to break lines within an ornamented character complex (cl-21) sequence. Also, it is prohibited to use inter-character spacing within an ornamented character complex (cl-21) sequence for line adjustment.
cases.rationale: The document states this prohibition three times and this case is the first of the three boundaries the third statement names. § 3.7.1 forbids the break in prose, § 3.1.10's ninth item repeats it as one of twelve unbreakable sequences — 'Between a subscript or superscript and an adjacent base character (preceding or following)' — and § C.2 note 6 states it as the matrix answer: 'There is no line break opportunity between two consecutive characters belonging to the same ornamented character complex (cl-21).' The three permitted entries record that no relaxation opens it. § C.3's four levels list what each one relaxes, some entries as whole classes and some as single characters, and every entry across all four lies in cl-03 through cl-13; cl-21 is named nowhere in § C.3, and its two mechanisms — a reclassification or an override of Table 2 alone — have nothing to apply to here under either reading. So the strictest and the loosest level answer alike, which is what these entries assert. This expectation states breakability and nothing else: the spacing at this boundary is § B.2 note 9's, which hands it back to § 3.7.1's solid setting, and the second half of the quoted sentence — that this spacing may not be used for line adjustment — is an expansion-ladder fact that Appendix E states and this case does not.

permitted.source: JLReq (C.3 Very loose, the loosest of the four levels, whose list does not name cl-21)
JLReq (C.3 read as an override of Table 2 alone rather than as a reclassification)

forbidden.why: Applying a general line-breaking algorithm to the boundary. UAX #14 finds no break between two Latin letters, but it finds one between two ideographs, so an implementation that does not know the complex breaks a Japanese ornamented run wherever its neighbors happen to allow it. § 3.7.1 forbids the break inside the sequence without exception, and § C.3 opens no level for it.

cases.quote: Between a subscript or superscript and an adjacent base character (preceding or following) (see Figure 87), or between base characters with ornament characters, or between ornament characters themselves. The reason is that these character sequences are to be handled as one object.
cases.rationale: The second of the three boundaries § 3.1.10's ninth item names, and the one a naive model of the construct does not have: the ornament here is followed by another base character of the same complex rather than by the base it hangs on. The item names that boundary twice over — 'an adjacent base character (preceding or following)' and 'between base characters with ornament characters' — and gives the reason, that the sequence is one object. § C.2 note 6 reaches the same answer from the run identity rather than from the roles, which is why an implementation only needs to know that the two occurrences are in the same complex.

cases.quote: Between a subscript or superscript and an adjacent base character (preceding or following) (see Figure 87), or between base characters with ornament characters, or between ornament characters themselves. The reason is that these character sequences are to be handled as one object.
cases.rationale: The third boundary of the same item: two ornament characters of one complex, here the first two digits of a mass number set before its element symbol. An implementation that stores one ornament per base character has no such boundary to answer and will break a multi-digit ornament across two lines. The complex is declared ornament-first because that is the § 3.7.1 exception a chemical formula takes, so this input carries both facts at once and an implementation that mishandles either answers it wrongly.

cases.quote: There is no line break opportunity between two consecutive characters belonging to the same ornamented character complex (cl-21). If two consecutive characters belong to different ornamented character complexes (cl-21), a line break opportunity exists between them.
cases.rationale: The other half of § C.2 note 6, and the reason the class is not enough to answer a boundary. Both occurrences at this boundary are cl-21, so a matrix indexed by the two classes alone reports one answer for it and for the boundary inside a complex, and one of the two is wrong. What separates them is the run: the same complex or a different one. Two complexes are declared here, adjacent, with no character between them, and the break opportunity exists. § B.2 note 9 draws the same distinction for the spacing and § E.2 note 5 for the expansion, so an implementation that carries run identity answers all three and one that carries only the class answers none.

forbidden.why: Answering from the class pair. Both occurrences are cl-21 and the boundary inside a complex is unbreakable, so an implementation that looks up cl-21 against cl-21 and stops denies this break — which would make two adjacent formulae one indivisible object and, in the limit, a line that cannot be broken at all. § C.2 note 6 conditions its two answers on the complex rather than on the class.
